title: Organizing a PHP Project
learning_outcomes: Explain what organizing a php project contributes to a PHP application.
Apply at least one of these concepts in a small example: source directories.
Check one edge case and explain how to diagnose unexpected behavior.

content.intro: Application architecture separates incoming requests, use-case rules, persistence, and external services. Patterns are useful when they clarify a dependency or invariant, not merely because they have a name. In this lesson, focus on source directories; then compare it with public document root. Use the example to predict a result before checking it, and record one case where the behavior may differ.
content.why_it_matters: You will use organizing a php project when building readable, testable PHP programs. Its practical value is knowing which rule applies, what result to expect, and how to handle failure or unexpected input.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Application architecture separates incoming requests, use-case rules, persistence, and external services. Patterns are useful when they clarify a dependency or invariant, not merely because they have a name. For organizing a php project, begin with source directories. Also distinguish public document root; configuration directories; tests and resources. Identify the input, the rule applied, and the observable output or side effect; then check the relevant official reference when a version or edge-case detail matters.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Use the smallest representative example, make expected behavior explicit, and test normal plus boundary inputs.

content_blocks.title: Walk through one example
content_blocks.text: Read the example for organizing a php project from top to bottom. Start by identifying source directories, write down the relevant variable values or control-flow choice, and predict the expected output before running it. Then change one input or condition, check a boundary case, and explain why the result changed.

task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes a clear use of source directories.
The learner can explain its input, rule, and observable output.
At least one edge case is tested or documented.
hints: Start with the most direct listed subtopic and a single input.
Keep the example small enough that you can predict the output manually.
Test one normal case and one empty, invalid, or boundary case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a pattern without understanding its inputs and output.
common_mistakes.why: Small environment or type differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Trace one example by hand, name expected outputs, and consult version-matched official docs.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring empty, invalid, or boundary input.
common_mistakes.why: Real data rarely matches only the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a deliberate edge-case check before relying on the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Making several changes at once while debugging.
common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify which change caused the behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Reduce the issue to one small reproducible case, change one cause, and retest.
